Retelling: A master going on a journey entrusted his property to his servants: five talents to one, two to another, one to another, each according to his ability. The first two traded and doubled their sums; the third dug a hole and buried his talent, then blamed his master's hardness for his fear. On return, the master praised the faithful servants — well done, good and faithful servant; you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much — and took the buried talent from the fearful one and gave it to the one with ten. Luke tells the same story as the parable of the minas, where a nobleman gives ten servants one mina each before travelling to receive a kingdom, and rewards or judges them on his return. In both versions the point is identical: what is entrusted must be put to work, and fear is no excuse for burying it.
Discussion: The master rewarded faithfulness, not size: the two-talent servant heard the same praise as the five-talent one. Only the servant who did nothing lost everything. Reflect: What talent — money, skill, opportunity, time — have you buried out of fear? Are you comparing your five with someone else's two instead of trading your own? What would faithful risk look like this month?
Significance: The talents teach stewardship: God entrusts gifts unequally but judges faithfulness equally, and fearful inaction is itself unfaithfulness.
